message:
QUESTION:
Under the council's affordability rule, can a median-income household in the city afford to buy the median house, or to rent a median 2-bedroom flat?

DATA:
City housing affordability, 2025.

- Median house price: £320,000. Lower-quartile house price: £230,000.
- Median gross household income: £40,000 a year. Median take-home (net) household income: £2,700 a month.
- Over the past year, median house prices rose 6% and median household incomes rose 3%.
- First-time-buyer assumptions: 10% deposit, 25-year capital-repayment mortgage at 5.0% fixed interest.
  - Monthly repayment on a £288,000 loan (median house): £1,684.
  - Monthly repayment on a £207,000 loan (lower-quartile house): £1,210.
- Median rent, 2-bedroom flat: £1,150 a month.
- Council affordability rule: housing costs are 'affordable' if they take no more than 35% of net (take-home) household income.
- Repayment figures use the standard repayment-mortgage formula and exclude insurance and maintenance. Rents exclude bills.
- Income figures cover all household types in the city.
- The council applies the 35% rule to both renting and buying.
- No data are available on planning permissions, housing supply, or who is buying homes in the city.

<analysis>
# Can a median-income household afford to buy or rent in the city?

**No, on either count.** Under the council's rule, housing costs must take no more than 35% of take-home income. For a median household, that is **£945 a month**. The median house, the lower-quartile house and the median 2-bedroom rent all cost more than that.

## Scope

This note applies the council's 35% rule to a household on the median take-home income of £2,700 a month, using 2025 figures. Mortgage repayments exclude insurance and maintenance, and rents exclude bills. Real housing costs are therefore higher than shown here, so these results are a best case.

## The test

| Option | Monthly cost | Share of £2,700 net income | Passes 35% test? | Net income needed to pass |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Buy median house (£320,000) | £1,684 | **62%** | No | £4,811/month |
| Buy lower-quartile house (£230,000) | £1,210 | **45%** | No | £3,457/month |
| Rent median 2-bed flat | £1,150 | **43%** | No | £3,286/month |
| *Affordable ceiling at median income* | *£945* | *35%* | n/a | n/a |

## Buying

**Repayments fail the test.** The median house needs a £288,000 loan. Over 25 years at 5.0%, that costs £1,684 a month, or about £505,000 in total. This is **62%** of median take-home pay, far above the 35% limit. To pass, a household would need net income of about £4,800 a month, nearly 80% more than the median.

The lower-quartile house also fails. A £207,000 loan costs £1,210 a month, which is **45%** of take-home pay.

**The deposit is a further barrier.** The council's 35% test covers only monthly costs, so the deposit is an extra hurdle outside the rule. A 10% deposit is £32,000 on the median house, about 12 months of median take-home pay. On the lower-quartile house it is £23,000, about 8½ months. The repayment figures above assume the household has already saved this.

## Renting

The median 2-bedroom rent of £1,150 is **43%** of median take-home pay. It fails the 35% test by about £205 a month.

Renting has the lowest monthly cost of the three options. Even so, the monthly figures alone do not show whether renting or buying is the better choice over time:
- Rent is only £60 a month less than repayments on the lower-quartile house (£1,150 against £1,210).
- Buying also needs a deposit and carries maintenance costs, which are not included here.
- Part of each mortgage repayment builds equity, which rent does not.

The rent figure excludes bills. The data do not say whether the council counts bills as "housing costs". If it does, renting fails the test by more than shown.

## A broader measure: price-to-income

The median house price is 8.0 times median gross household income (£320,000 ÷ £40,000). Ratios above about 5 are often described as "severely unaffordable", for example in Demographia's international housing affordability survey. This benchmark is not part of the council's rule, but it points the same way.

## Trend

Over the past year, median house prices rose 6% and median incomes rose 3%. Working back from these rates, the price-to-income ratio was about 7.8 a year ago (roughly £302,000 ÷ £38,800). It is 8.0 now. **On this measure, buying became less affordable.**

The council's rule depends on monthly repayments, which also depend on mortgage rates. Last year's rates are not given:
- **If rates were also 5% a year ago,** repayments rose about 6% while incomes rose 3%. The repayment share for the median house would then have risen from about 61% to 62%, so buying also became less affordable under the council's rule. This assumes take-home income grew at the same rate as gross income.
- **If rates were higher a year ago,** lower rates now may have offset the price rise. Repayment affordability may then have held steady or improved.

No rent trend data are given, so the direction for renters cannot be assessed.

## Causes

The 5% interest rate directly drives the repayment figures shown here. The data do not show why house prices are high or why they are rising faster than incomes. Possible explanations include constrained supply and demand from investors or incoming households. No data are available on planning permissions, housing supply or who is buying homes, so these explanations cannot be tested here. Choosing the right policy response would need that evidence.

## Conclusions

1. **Buying the median house is clearly unaffordable** for a median household. Repayments take 62% of take-home pay, against a 35% limit. Even a lower-quartile house fails, at 45%. The deposit, about a year's take-home pay for the median house, is a further hurdle outside the council's test.
2. **Renting a median 2-bedroom flat is also unaffordable**, at 43% of take-home pay. It is the cheapest of the three options each month, but it still fails the council's test.
3. **House prices rose faster than incomes over the past year**, so the price-to-income ratio worsened from 7.8 to 8.0. If mortgage rates were unchanged, repayment affordability under the council's rule also worsened. Last year's rates are needed to confirm this.
4. **The real affordability gap is larger than shown**, because these figures exclude insurance, maintenance and bills.

## Caveats

- The figures describe a household on exactly the median income. Households above the median, or with existing equity or savings, will be better placed. Households below the median will be worse placed.
- The income figures cover all household types. Renters typically earn less than owners, so a median *renting* household is likely to spend more than 43% of its income on rent.
- A 2-bedroom flat may be more or less space than a given household needs.
</analysis>

Produce the final version of this analysis.
